extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers, especially those writing horror
extracted.subtask_description: Genre-specific quality criteria for writing horror fiction, covering core elements (atmosphere, psychological depth, pacing, restraint, character vulnerability, monster design) and practical quality-check questions for drafts. Useful for short stories and longer fiction across multiple horror subgenres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere & Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant tonal register; established from the first sentence through setting, word choice, sentence rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality horror sustains unease across the work. Establish tone early (often from the first sentence) and maintain consistent choices in setting, diction, and sentence rhythm to keep readers in a state of dread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological Depth Over Surface Scares
rubrics_metrics.description: Best horror exploits internal fears — guilt, paranoia, isolation, loss of identity, insanity — rather than relying on jump scares or gore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize characters' inner lives and emotional stakes; the page's maxim: 'The real can be scarier than the surreal.' Avoid cheap shocks that have no emotional or thematic grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatable Characters & Settings
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrast between ordinary settings (suburban home, summer camp, hospital) and shocking events amplifies fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must be sufficiently fleshed-out for readers to fear for them. Use familiar, everyday places to heighten the sense that horror can intrude on the normal world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing — Tension Building & Release
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror requires lulls (where dread builds) interrupted by intensity (the scene of revelation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is crucial: endless intensity exhausts the reader; pure dread without payoff frustrates. Structure scenes so tension can accumulate and occasionally release for maximum impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint — The Unseen
rubrics_metrics.description: Implication is more frightening than description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow principles like Lovecraft's: withhold explicit detail and let the reader's imagination supply horrors. Avoid over-describing the monster or event; suggestion often increases terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonists must be able to lose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invulnerable or superheroic characters cannot sustain horror because stakes disappear. Ensure your central characters have believable weaknesses and stakes that make danger meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing on Personal Fears
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic fears (clowns, etc.) feel rote; specific personal fears (your worst memory, your private shame) generate fresh horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine personal, particular anxieties and experiences to create original, resonant fear rather than relying on overused tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Right Monster
rubrics_metrics.description: The monster (literal or metaphorical) must embody something larger — the era's anxieties, the protagonist's repressed fear, social pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design antagonists or threats that symbolize thematic concerns. The monster should feel narratively necessary, not arbitrarily terrifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Cosmic horror
rubrics_metrics.description: The universe is indifferent or malevolent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/authors: Lovecraft, Thomas Ligotti. Use cosmic scale and existential dread rather than human-scale threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Psychological horror
rubrics_metrics.description: The threat may be internal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/authors: Shirley Jackson, Henry James. Blurs lines between reality and perception; focuses on mental states and unreliable experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmosphere of decay and isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/authors: Daphne du Maurier, Cormac McCarthy. Use setting and mood (ruins, mansions, bleak landscapes) to generate dread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Slasher
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodied antagonist and body horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/works: King's Misery, Halloween novelizations. Emphasizes a physical, often human, antagonist and scenes of bodily threat or violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Folk horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Rural horror rooted in local belief and tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/works: The Wicker Man, Adam Nevill. Leverage community rituals, folklore, and isolation to create dread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Body horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical transformation or violation as the source of horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/authors/filmmakers: David Cronenberg, Carmen Maria Machado. Focus on the grotesque and the breakdown of the human body or identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Quiet horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic and suggestive horror that emphasizes subtlety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/works/authors: Carmilla, du Maurier. Often set in everyday domestic spaces and relies on implication and mood rather than spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Splatterpunk
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme, transgressive horror emphasizing graphic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example author: Clive Barker. Prioritizes shock and transgression; suited to readers expecting explicitness and boundary-pushing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre — Post-modern horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-aware horror that plays with form and reader expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example work: Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves. Employs unconventional structure, unreliable narration, and self-referential devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Opening establishes dread
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the opening establish dread?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative checkpoint: the opening should set tone and begin to seed unease immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Sustained atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Does atmosphere sustain across the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen tone and mood remain coherent and effective from start to finish, without jarring shifts that dissipate fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Scares are earned
rubrics_metrics.description: Are scares earned by setup?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for narrative setup that justifies frightening moments; avoid unmotivated shocks that feel gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Source of horror is specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the source of horror specific (not generic)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the threat connects to particular anxieties, characters, or themes rather than resting on clichéd or vague fears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Horror reflects deeper anxiety or theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Does horror reflect a deeper anxiety or theme?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the horror resonates thematically—e.g., social, psychological, or existential concerns—rather than being purely sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Ending leaves the right residue
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the ending leave the right residue (relief, dread, ambiguity)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the ending's emotional tone matches the story's aims—providing catharsis, lingering dread, or purposeful ambiguity as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Reader fears for the character
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the reader fear for the character?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical checkpoint: if readers aren't invested enough to worry about the protagonist's fate, the horror's stakes are weakened.
